summary: TerraLuna Atlas is a simple atlas that matches places on the Moon and Mars with similar places on Earth. Before a mission flies, teams test their tools on Earth, but the same few sites are used again and again. We took NASA’s Artemis South Pole regions and Mars targets like Gale, Gusev, Jezero and Arcadia. We paired each one with an Earth site, such as Haughton Crater, Lava Beds, Qaidam Basin, Dallol and Lake Salda. We compare the sites by their rocks, climate, resources like ice and lava tubes, and how easy they are to reach. We show the result on a world map and a comparison table. We also list where Earth is different, such as gravity, air and radiation. This gives mission teams more places to test and helps lower cost and risk.
details:
What does it do? TerraLuna Atlas pairs Moon and Mars targets with Earth sites that are similar. It shows the pairs on a world map and in a table. It also says what each site can test, and what it cannot.

How does it work? First, we pick a target from NASA data, such as the Artemis South Pole regions or Gale Crater. Second, we collect facts about Earth sites from NASA pages and published studies. Third, we compare each site by four things: geology, climate extremes, resources (ice, brines, lava tubes), and how practical it is to reach. Fourth, we put the results on a map and in a table. We did not write code. We used NASA web tools and public research.

What benefits does it have? It gives mission teams more places to test, beyond the sites that are used all the time. It shows which tools suit each site, such as drills, gas sensors, rovers and radar. It also shows what still needs a lab test.

What is the intended impact? We want to lower the cost and risk of space missions by testing the right tool in the right place before launch. We hope it gives planners a useful shortlist to build on. These are our goals, not measured results.

What tools did we use? We used NASA’s Planetary Analog Explorer, NASA’s pages on planetary analogs and Artemis landing regions, the NASA-funded SWIM ice maps, and Curiosity radiation results. We used Natural Earth data for the map. We used an AI assistant (Claude) for research, writing and building the slides and map. There was no hardware and no coding on our side.

How is it creative? We compare sites using measured numbers, not just how they look. We include less-known sites like Qaidam Basin and Dallol next to famous NASA ones. Every site also comes with a note on where the comparison fails. Everything is in one map and one table.

What factors did we consider? Rock and mineral types, slope, temperature, dryness, ground ice and brines, lava tubes for shelter, wind and water, access and safety, what equipment can be tested, and the differences in gravity, air pressure, radiation and water.
